oneLineAnswer: Remdesivir is an intravenous antiviral medicine a healthcare provider gives for COVID-19, mostly in hospital or infusion settings.
whatItIs: Remdesivir is an antiviral medicine sold under the brand name Veklury. It is a prescription product, not a supplement, and the approved product is given only through a vein. The label calls it an adenosine nucleotide prodrug, meaning the body turns it into the working molecule. It ships as a powder that is mixed with sterile water and then saline before infusion. Its molecular formula is C27H35N6O8P and its molecular weight is about 602.6.
whatItDoes: It blocks an enzyme the coronavirus needs to copy its RNA, its genetic material.
Inside cells it turns into an active form that mimics a natural RNA building block.
That mimic gets built into the growing viral chain, which stalls the copying.
In a trial of hospitalized adults, median time to recovery was 10 days with remdesivir and 15 days with placebo.
The same trial reported 29-day mortality of 11% with remdesivir and 15% with placebo.
howPeopleUseIt: A healthcare provider gives it by intravenous infusion, and the label says never by another route.
It is given where staff can act on a severe reaction right away, not by you at home.
The label records a 3-day course for some non-hospitalized patients.
For hospitalized patients on a ventilator, the label records up to 10 days.
The label records an infusion time of 30 to 120 minutes.

commonSideEffects: Nausea is the reaction the label lists most often.
Blood tests may show higher liver enzymes, reported as ALT increased and AST increased.
The label says nausea, ALT increased and AST increased were seen in at least 5% of treated people.
seriousSigns: Allergic reactions can start during or after the infusion, and the label says most happened within one hour.
Other listed signs include blood pressure changes, abnormal heart rate, low blood oxygen, fever, wheezing, swelling, rash and shivering.
The label says to consider stopping treatment if liver enzymes rise above 10 times the normal upper limit.
One seizure and a few cases of acute kidney injury appear in the label's tables of trial events.
whoShouldAvoid: The label rules it out after a serious allergic reaction to the drug or an ingredient.

interactions: Chloroquine phosphate and hydroxychloroquine sulfate should not be given with remdesivir, the label says.
The reason is lab evidence that chloroquine may work against remdesivir's activation inside cells.
The label expects no important interaction with the liver enzyme CYP3A4 or with several drug transporters it studied.
Remdesivir is described as a weak inhibitor of the liver enzyme CYP3A.
The label tells patients to report all prescription drugs, nonprescription drugs and herbal products they take.
pregnancyAndChildren: Available data have not linked it to birth defects, miscarriage, or poor outcomes in the second and third trimesters. The label says there are not enough data to judge first-trimester exposure. It also says no dose change is recommended in pregnancy. Untreated COVID-19 in pregnancy carries risks of its own for the mother and baby. One published case report found remdesivir and its active metabolite in human milk. Reports on 11 breastfed infants did not indicate harm from exposure through milk. There are no data on whether it affects milk production. Use is established for children from birth to under 18 years who weigh at least 1.5 kg. No data are available on safety in children with severe kidney impairment.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether the results still apply the same way now: the label notes the main trial's subjects were unvaccinated.
The label says the drug's share of a liver enzyme rise versus COVID-19 is hard to tell.
The label does not describe effects beyond the treatment period.
Liver-injury detail from the NIDDK LiverTox page is missing; that page blocked our fetch with a browser check.
Later treatment recommendations from bodies other than the FDA are outside the sources checked here.
The label gives different enrollment numbers for the same trial in different sections; we did not try to reconcile them.
No fetched source compares remdesivir head to head with other COVID-19 treatments.

gaps: NCCIH has no remdesivir page: the URL supplied for this task returned HTTP 404, and the NCCIH COVID-19 complementary-approaches page yielded no remdesivir facts we could cite.
NCBI Bookshelf (LiverTox, NIDDK) served a browser check on three attempts, so no liver-injury detail from that public-domain source is cited.
MedlinePlus had no drug or condition page naming remdesivir at the URLs tried; its coronavirus infections topic page links to treatment pages but does not name this drug.
No permitted source we could fetch compares remdesivir with other COVID-19 treatments, so no comparative claim is made.
The label reports both 532 and 541 as the treated arm size in its own description of the main trial; we cite the trial registry figure of 1062 total participants instead of picking a label number.
No dose, schedule or personal protocol is stated here by design; only what the label and trials recorded is reported, attributed.
No fetched source describes long-term effects after a short course, and the label does not cover them.
summary: This record covers what remdesivir (Veklury) is, how it is given, what the FDA label and its main trial reported about benefit and risk in COVID-19, and where the fetched sources stay silent.
